hero.name: Roshni
hero.who: a 34-year-old home baker in Kochi whose customers only come for discounts

story.b: Roshni bakes from her flat kitchen in Kakkanad, Kochi, and sells through Instagram. Her banana bread is soft, her plum cake is rich, and her customers mostly vanish the moment an offer ends. Twenty percent off brings a busy weekend. Then the phone goes quiet. Last month a new bakery opened near Edappally with lower prices and shinier photos, and her orders dropped again. She sits up past midnight with a calculator, and the margins are thinner than her icing. Her husband asks a simple question over a late dinner. What makes your cakes different? Roshni lists butter, eggs, delivery timings and prices. As she says it, she hears how much it sounds like every other bakery in the city.

ask.q: Roshni keeps needing discounts to get orders. What should she work on first?
o: Offer a bigger discount than the new bakery to win customers back
Post more often so her name stays in people's feeds
Work out why she bakes at all, beyond money, and lead with that
ask.why: Bigger discounts start a price war she cannot win, and more posts only repeat the same menu and prices louder. Customers who come for offers leave when offers end. Knowing her real reason for baking gives people something to care about besides the price.

chapters.take: If you only talk about price, price is all people will remember.

story.h: A notebook after the oven cools
story.b: One night, after the oven cools, Roshni opens an old notebook and writes one question at the top. Why do I bake? The first answers are about money. She crosses them out. Then she remembers her grandmother's kitchen in Thrissur, where every birthday cake was baked for one person, with their name piped in wobbly letters. Nobody ever bought those cakes. They were made because someone mattered. Roshni writes a sentence: I believe a celebration cake should feel like it was made by someone who knows you. It sounds small, but it is true. She rewrites her Instagram bio, and her next post talks about why she still writes every name by hand, before it mentions the menu.

ask.q: Roshni is rewriting her Instagram bio. Which opening fits the idea best?
o: Start with her belief that celebration cakes should feel personal and homemade
Start with her full menu so people know exactly what she sells
Start with her lowest prices, since that is what people search for
ask.why: Menus and prices tell people what she does, and every bakery does that. Her belief tells them why, which is what makes someone stop scrolling and feel something. The menu still matters, but it lands better after the why.

chapters.take: Start with why you do it. What you sell comes after.

story.b: As Christmas comes near, a delivery app agent calls Roshni with an offer. List her plum cake with a forty percent flash sale, a countdown clock and a banner saying only three left. Orders will flood in, he promises. Roshni thinks of last year's offer crowd, who bought once and never came back. She has plenty of cakes, so the banner would be a lie. She thanks him and declines. Instead she messages her past customers. She tells them the fruit has been soaking in her kitchen since October, that she bakes each cake herself in small batches, and that she will stop when she runs out. Orders come in slowly. Several people ask to book for next year too.

ask.q: The app suggests a banner saying only three cakes left, though she has plenty. What should Roshni do?
o: Use the banner just this once, since everyone does it at festival time
Skip the fake pressure and tell customers honestly why her cake is special
Use the banner and add a free gift, so the deal feels even bigger
ask.why: A fake countdown can pull a crowd once, but it trains people to buy out of pressure, not because of her. When they notice the trick, trust drops. Telling the honest story of her cake brings fewer but warmer orders, from people likely to return.

chapters.take: Pressure brings a crowd once. Purpose brings people back.

story.b: Roshni notices that some customers never wait for offers. Mrs Mathew, a retired teacher from Panampilly Nagar, orders a cake every month. One day, while handing over the box, Roshni asks her why. Mrs Mathew taps the lid and says Roshni wrote her husband's name, and remembered he cannot eat walnuts. Roshni realises her regulars are not just buying cake. They are buying the feeling of being known, and they share her belief that celebrations should be personal. So she starts a small Sunday tasting on her building's terrace, once a month, where regulars try new recipes and give honest opinions. They bring friends. Soon they talk about Roshni's cakes as if the bakery partly belongs to them.

ask.q: Roshni wants more customers like Mrs Mathew. What is the best next step?
o: Offer Mrs Mathew a big loyalty discount so she keeps ordering
Copy the trendy cakes the new bakery sells, to look modern
Ask regulars why they choose her, and build more of that shared feeling
ask.why: Her regulars do not stay for discounts; they share her belief that cakes should feel personal. A discount turns them into deal hunters, and copying trends hides what makes her different. Learning what they value lets her offer more of it and draw in people who feel the same.

chapters.take: People belong where someone believes what they believe.

story.b: In January, an IT office in Infopark calls with a big order. Two hundred cupcakes for an event tomorrow, at a price that would cover two months of rent. The catch is speed. They want them from a ready premix, topped with plastic decorations, in plain boxes with no names. Roshni almost says yes. Then she looks at the sentence pinned above her oven, about cakes made by someone who knows you. A premix cupcake for strangers, rushed overnight, does not fit. She calls back and offers sixty cupcakes, baked her way, with a handwritten card for the team, delivered by Friday. The office manager hesitates, then agrees. Two employees later order birthday cakes for their own families.

ask.q: A big office wants two hundred premix cupcakes by tomorrow. How should Roshni decide?
o: Take it, since a big order matters more than values right now
Check it against her why, and offer what she can make her way
Take it but hide the premix, so her image stays safe
ask.why: Her why is real only if her choices match it. Used as a filter, it shows her the order does not fit, and she can offer a version that does. Taking it blindly blurs what she stands for, and hiding the premix breaks the trust she is building.

chapters.take: Your purpose only counts if your choices match it.

story.b: By March, Roshni has two helpers, Ammu, a college student, and Salma from the flat next door. Orders are growing, and Roshni spends more time on accounts and deliveries than on baking. One afternoon she sees a box going out with a printed sticker instead of a handwritten name. Ammu says it is faster, and she is right. Roshni realises that nobody ever told the helpers why the names matter. She has been so busy growing that the reason stayed in her own head. That Sunday she makes chai for both of them, opens her old notebook and tells them about her grandmother's kitchen. The next morning Ammu writes every name by hand and adds a tiny star.

ask.q: Her helpers are skipping handwritten names to save time. What should Roshni do?
o: Sit with them and share why she started and why the names matter
Make a strict rule and cut pay for anyone who skips a name
Let it go, since faster boxes mean more orders and growth
ask.why: The helpers are not careless; nobody told them the reason. Sharing the story turns a rule into something they care about. Pay cuts get grudging obedience, and letting it slide lets the purpose fade quietly as the business grows.

chapters.take: As you grow, keep telling the story of why you started.

story.b: By the next Christmas, Roshni has not run a single discount in months. The new bakery near Edappally still flashes offers every weekend. Her plum cake list closed in November, and the waiting list has names she has never met, sent by people who have. The Sunday terrace tasting has become a small crowd with folding chairs. Ammu now writes names more neatly than Roshni does. When a new customer messages asking about price, Roshni first tells them a little about how and why she bakes. Most of them never ask for a discount. Her husband asks the old question again over dinner, what makes your cakes different. This time she answers in one sentence.

chapters.take: People stay for what you believe, not for what you discount.
